source_text: Commentarius in Psalmum 92 (fragmenta) ΕΡΜΗΝΕΙΑ ΤΟΥ 92 ΨΑΛΜΟΥ 35 Πρόδηλον οὖν εἴπερ ὁ χρίων ἀποδεικνύει Θεὸν οὗ τὸν θρόνον εἶπεν αἰώνιον, δῆλος μέν ἐστι φύσει Θεὸς ἐκ Θεοῦ γεννηθεὶς ὁ χρίσας, ὁ δὲ χρισθεὶς ἐπίκτητον εἴληφεν ἀρετὴν ἐκκρίτῳ ναουργίᾳ κοσμηθεὶς ἐκ τῆς τοῦ κατοικοῦντος ἐν αὐτῷ θεότητος. 36 Πέρας γοῦν ὁ προφήτης Ἡσαΐας αὐτὰ μὲν τὰ τῶν παθῶν αὐτοῦ διεξιὼν ἴχνη πρὸς τοῖς ἄλλοις ἐπιφέρει καὶ τοῦτο μεγαλοφωνοτέρᾳ βοῇ, τό· καὶ εἴδομεν αὐτὸν καὶ οὐκ εἶχεν οὔτε εἶδος οὔτε κάλλος· ἀλλὰ τὸ εἶδος αὐτοῦ ἄτιμον καὶ ἐκλεῖπον παρὰ τοὺς υἱοὺς τῶν ἀνθρώπων.
thought_title: The anointed man's dishonor, not the indwelling God's
orientation: Eustathius has just distinguished the one who anoints (God by nature) from the anointed one (the man who receives acquired virtue), and now cites Isaiah's description of the suffering servant's lack of appearance and beauty.
pass_a_gloss: It is clear therefore, if indeed the one who anoints proves to be God whose throne he said was eternal, the one who anointed is clearly God by nature begotten from God, but the anointed one received acquired virtue, adorned by the divinity of the indwelling God with a special fashioning of a temple. At any rate the prophet Isaiah, going through the very traces of his sufferings, brings forward among the other things also this with a louder cry, namely: and we saw him and he had neither appearance nor beauty; but his appearance was dishonored and failing compared to the sons of men.

pass_b_english: It is clear, then, that if the one who anoints proves God—the one whose throne the psalmist called eternal—then the one who anoints is evidently God by nature, begotten from God. The anointed one, however, received acquired virtue, adorned by the exceptional fashioning of a temple through the divinity of the God dwelling in him.

At any rate, the prophet Isaiah, when he goes through the very traces of his sufferings, adds this among other things with a louder cry: “We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty; but his appearance was without honor, lacking, beyond the sons of men” (Isaiah 53:2-3).

problems.source_quote: καὶ εἴδομεν αὐτὸν καὶ οὐκ εἶχεν οὔτε εἶδος οὔτε κάλλος· ἀλλὰ τὸ εἶδος αὐτοῦ ἄτιμον καὶ ἐκλεῖπον παρὰ τοὺς υἱοὺς τῶν ἀνθρώπων
problems.why: The quotation matches LXX Isaiah 53:2-3, but the citation says only 'Isaiah 53:2'. The source quotation includes material from both verse 2 ('neither appearance nor beauty') and verse 3 ('dishonored and failing beyond the sons of men'). The brief specifies to cite as 'Isaiah 53:2-3'. English cites only 53:2, omitting verse 3.

Re-checking: ἀποδεικνύει takes accusative Θεὸν, meaning 'proves/demonstrates/shows God' (object), not 'proves to be God' (predicate nominative). The English 'proves to be God' makes the subject ('the one who anoints') into God, whereas Greek says he demonstrates/proves God (the Father? or the divine nature?). This is a significant change in meaning and agency.
problems.ruling: ἀποδεικνύει Θεὸν means 'proves/demonstrates God' (accusative object), not 'proves to be God' (predicate), changing agency and meaning.
